ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) is a precancerous lesion of the vulvar epithelium that can progress to invasive vulvar cancer if untreated. It is identified by abnormal cells confined to the epithelium and graded by severity.

sections.p: VIN is a squamous intraepithelial lesion of the vulva with atypical keratinocytes that do not invade the basement membrane. Diagnosis requires a biopsy showing dysplasia and exclusion of invasive carcinoma.
b: Biopsy is the gold standard; visual inspection alone is insufficient.
Immunohistochemistry (p16) helps identify HPV‑related lesions.

sections.p: VIN is graded as usual type (uVIN) – HPV‑related, or differentiated type (dVIN) – HPV‑independent. uVIN uses a three‑tier system (VIN 1‑3); dVIN is considered high‑grade by definition.
b: VIN 1 = mild dysplasia (often regresses).
VIN 2 = moderate dysplasia.
VIN 3 = severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ.
dVIN = high‑grade, higher risk of progression.

sections.p: Most VIN cases are driven by persistent high‑risk HPV infection, especially types 16 and 18. Differentiated VIN is linked to chronic dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus and immunosuppression (e.g., HIV).
b: HPV infection (high‑risk types).
Lichen sclerosus or other chronic vulvar dermatoses.
Immunosuppression (HIV, organ transplant).
Smoking – a co‑factor for HPV persistence.

sections.p: Patients may notice a persistent, often asymptomatic, white or pigmented patch, papule, or ulcer on the vulva. It can be itchy, painful, or bleed, especially after friction.
b: Often discovered incidentally during routine exam.
Lesions may be multifocal.
Symptoms are nonspecific; high index of suspicion needed.

sections.p: Targeted testing confirms diagnosis, assesses HPV status, and rules out invasion.

t.b: Does the lesion contain dysplastic cells confined to epithelium?

t.a: HPV DNA testing (PCR or in‑situ hybridisation)

t.b: Does the lesion show over‑expression of p16?
What is the extent of the lesion?

sections.p: Unrecognized or untreated high‑grade VIN can evolve into invasive vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, which carries morbidity and mortality.
b: Rapid growth, ulceration, or fixation to underlying tissue.
Persistent pain or bleeding.
Lymphadenopathy suggests invasion.

sections.p: Treatment aims to eradicate dysplasia while preserving function. Options depend on grade, size, and patient factors.
b: Topical imiquimod for small, HPV‑related VIN 1‑2 (immune modulation).
Surgical excision (wide local excision) for VIN 2‑3 or dVIN (complete removal).
Laser ablation or CO₂ laser for selected lesions.
Avoid cryotherapy alone for high‑grade disease (high recurrence).

sections.p: Regular surveillance is essential because recurrence and new lesions are common.
b: Examine vulva every 3–6 months for 2 years, then annually.
HPV vaccination (if not already immunised) reduces future risk.
Smoking cessation and control of lichen sclerosus lower recurrence.

sections.p: Several benign or malignant conditions can mimic VIN.
b: Lichen sclerosus – white atrophic patches without dysplasia.
Vulvar intra‑mucosal melanoma – pigmented lesion, requires different pathology.
Condyloma acuminatum – HPV warts, usually low‑grade.

sections.p: Certain tests may give false reassurance.
b: Negative HPV test does not exclude dVIN.
p16 may be focally positive in non‑HPV lesions, requiring correlation with morphology.
Biopsy sampling error can miss focal invasion; consider repeat biopsy if suspicion persists.

whenToSeekHelp: New onset pain or foul discharge

faq.a: Low‑grade (VIN 1) lesions may regress, especially if risk factors are removed, but high‑grade VIN rarely does.

faq.q: Is HPV vaccination useful after a VIN diagnosis?
faq.a: Vaccination does not treat existing VIN but can protect against future HPV‑related lesions.

faq.q: What is the difference between uVIN and dVIN?
faq.a: uVIN is HPV‑related, often multifocal, and occurs in younger women; dVIN is HPV‑independent, linked to chronic dermatoses, and has higher malignant potential.

exam: Describe the histopathologic criteria that differentiate VIN from invasive vulvar cancer.
Explain why dVIN carries a higher risk of progression than uVIN.
Outline the management algorithm for a patient with multifocal VIN 2.
